newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Huge crowds in Hong Kong mourn Tiananmen victims.
newsitem.headline: Huge crowds in Hong Kong mourn Tiananmen victims.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Hong Kong people honoured the victims of the bloody 1989 Beijing crackdown on Wednesday, just 27 days before the British colony reverts to communist-ruled China.

While authorities over the border in China staged a security clampdown to avert anniversary protests, more than 55,000 Hong Kong people flocked to a candlelit vigil on the eighth anniversary of the June 4 massacre around Tiananmen Square.
In a park named after Britain's 19th century empress, Queeen Victoria, a towering grey "Pillar of Shame" statue of twisted human bodies depicting oppression stood spotlit in the dark.
Some mourners wept as they sang rousing pro-democracy anthems. Other pumped their arms defiantly in the air and vowed to return year after year.

Many Hong Kong people fear their peaceful yet poignant annual tribute to the victims of Tiananmen will be outlawed after Britain hands its wealthy colony of 6.4 million people over to China at midnight on June 30.

The singing swelled as the grandfather of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement Szeto Wah, dubbed a subversive by China, set a torch ablaze and vowed the spirit of June 4 would live on beyond the handover.
"Eight years, 2,922 days and nights, have passed. Tonight we are again using sparks of candlelight, solidified drops of tears, to remember to you and to mourn you," read one tribute.
Simon So, who said he had missed only one rally in the past eight years, brought his five year old daughter along. "The next generation must be taught never to forget," So, a computer engineer, said.

"I think some people think it's the last time that it will be allowed but most people will come, they will just come next year," said Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's Democracy Party and a founding member of the Hong Kong Alliance.

More than one million Hong Kong people took to the streets in June 1989 to express shock and revulsion over the brutality of their future leaders. The crackdown sparked a middle class exodus from Hong Kong and gave birth to the democracy movement.

Exiled Chinese dissident Han Dongfang, jailed for his part in the Tiananmen protests, vowed the movement would soldier on. "I believe many Hong Kong people will connect together on this day to support the democracy movement in China," said Han who plans to stay in Hong Kong beyond the handover and hopes one day to return to China.
Activists denounced Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa, Beijing's appointee to run Hong Kong when Britain withdraws, for urging people to forget the "June 4 baggage" and look forward.
"Mr Tung should have come here tonight to see how peaceful the people are," said Lee, who was mobbed by autograph hunters.
Lee has angered Tung by campaigning overseas against Tung's plans, endorsed by China to dilute civil liberties, including curbs of demonstrations in the name of social stability.
"Mr Tung should go to see the Beijing leaders and ask them to reverse the verdict of June 4," Lee said.
"It was not a counter-revolutionary or criminal movement. It was a patriotic movement."
